stem: Which entry records the annual depreciation charge?

options.content: Debit income statement; credit provision for depreciation
options.rationale: Correct: an expense, and the provision builds up.

options.content: Debit provision for depreciation; credit income statement
options.rationale: This is the reverse entry.

options.content: Debit income statement; credit the asset account
options.rationale: The asset account stays at cost.

options.content: Debit the asset account; credit bank
options.rationale: This records buying the asset.

explanation: Depreciation is an expense (debit) and the provision for depreciation is credited.

stem: What is the normal balance on a provision for depreciation account?

options.content: A credit balance
options.rationale: Correct: it is built up by credits each year.

options.content: A debit balance
options.rationale: Assets at cost have debit balances; the provision offsets them.

options.content: No balance; it is closed each year
options.rationale: The provision is carried forward and grows each year.

options.content: Either side, depending on profit
options.rationale: Profit does not affect the side of the provision.

explanation: The provision account accumulates the depreciation charged so far, as a credit balance.

stem: Where is the balance on the provision for depreciation account shown?

options.content: As an expense in the income statement, below gross profit
options.rationale: Only this year's charge is an expense.

options.content: Deducted from the asset's cost in the statement of financial position
options.rationale: Correct: cost less accumulated depreciation gives net book value.

options.content: As a current liability
options.rationale: Nothing is owed; the provision reduces an asset.

options.content: Added to the owner's capital
options.rationale: The provision is not part of capital.

explanation: The provision is a contra-asset: it is subtracted from cost in the statement of financial position.

stem: Why is the non-current asset account kept at cost rather than reduced by depreciation each year?

options.content: Because depreciation is not a real expense
options.rationale: Depreciation is a real (non-cash) expense.

options.content: Because the value of a non-current asset never changes once bought
options.rationale: The value does fall; the fall is shown in the provision account.

options.content: So that the trial balance has fewer accounts
options.rationale: It actually adds an account (the provision).

options.content: So the original cost and the total depreciation can both be seen
options.rationale: Correct: users see what was paid and how much has been used up.

explanation: Separating cost and accumulated depreciation gives more information in the statement of financial position.

stem: A trial balance at 31 December 2025 shows machinery at cost US\$54,000 and provision for depreciation US\$19,440. Machinery is depreciated at 20% per annum on the reducing balance. What is the depreciation charge for 2025?

options.rationale: This is 20% of cost: the straight-line answer.
This is 20% of the provision brought forward.
This is the closing provision, not this year's charge.

hints: Reducing balance applies the rate to cost less the provision brought forward.

stem: A bookkeeper credited this year's depreciation of US\$3,000 to the equipment account instead of to the provision for depreciation account. What is the effect on the statement of financial position?

options.content: Net book value is overstated by US\$3,000
options.rationale: The 3,000 was still deducted, just from the wrong account.

options.content: Net book value is correct; cost and accumulated depreciation are both US\$3,000 too low
options.rationale: Correct: the deduction is in the wrong account, so the net figure is unchanged.

options.content: Profit is overstated by US\$3,000
options.rationale: The debit to the income statement was correct.

options.content: Total non-current assets are understated by US\$6,000, because both columns are too low
options.rationale: Cost is 3,000 too low but accumulated depreciation is also 3,000 too low.

explanation: Cost is 3,000 too low and the provision 3,000 too low, so the net book value is still correct, but the presentation is wrong.
hints: Net book value = cost − accumulated depreciation.

stem: The income statement shows the total depreciation charged on an asset since it was bought.
explanation: False. The income statement shows only this year's charge; the total is in the statement of financial position.

stem: In a trial balance, the provision for depreciation normally appears in the credit column.
explanation: True. It is a credit balance that reduces the debit balance of the asset.

stem: Complete the journal entry for depreciation of fixtures of US\$1,850 for the year.
explanation: Expense debited; provision credited. The fixtures account is not touched.

stem: Match each item with where it appears.

left.content: Closing balance of the provision for depreciation

right.content: Statement of financial position, deducted from cost
Statement of financial position, net book value column
Statement of financial position, cost column

explanation: One year's charge is an expense; cost, accumulated depreciation and net book value appear in the statement of financial position.

stem: Office furniture cost US\$28,800 on 1 January 2023. It is depreciated at 12.5% per annum on cost. What is the balance on the provision for depreciation account at 31 December 2025?

On 1 January 2025 Farai's equipment at cost was US\$42,000. On 1 September 2025 he bought more equipment for US\$18,000. Equipment is depreciated at 10% per annum on cost, on a monthly basis. Calculate the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2025.
explanation: Opening equipment: 10% × 42,000 = 4,200. New equipment: 10% × 18,000 × 4/12 = 600. Total 4,800. Charging a full year on the new equipment gives 6,000; ignoring it gives 4,200.
workedSolution: 1. Opening equipment: 10% × 42,000 = 4,200. New equipment: 10% × 18,000 × 4/12 = 600. Total 4,800. Charging a full year on the new equipment gives 6,000; ignoring it gives 4,200.
hints: Charge a full year on the opening cost.
The new equipment was owned for September to December.

stem: At 31 December 2025, before year-end adjustments, a trial balance shows motor vehicles at cost US\$64,500 and provision for depreciation US\$21,930. Depreciation for 2025 is US\$8,510. Calculate the net book value of motor vehicles to be shown in the statement of financial position.
explanation: Closing provision 21,930 + 8,510 = 30,440. NBV 64,500 − 30,440 = 34,060. Using the trial balance provision only gives 42,570.
workedSolution: 1. Closing provision 21,930 + 8,510 = 30,440. NBV 64,500 − 30,440 = 34,060. Using the trial balance provision only gives 42,570.
hints: The trial balance provision is the opening figure.

stem: Explain the difference between the depreciation charge for the year and the balance on the provision for depreciation account.

points.description: The charge is the depreciation for this year only, an expense in the income statement
The provision balance is the total depreciation charged since the asset was bought, deducted from cost in the statement of financial position

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The charge is this year's expense in the income statement; the provision is the accumulated total of all years' charges, deducted from cost in the statement of financial position.

explanation: One year versus all years to date.

parts.stem: Thandeka's accounts clerk suggests showing only net book values to save space. Which accounting concept is best served by showing cost and accumulated depreciation as well?

options.content: Going concern, because the assets will be used for many years
options.rationale: Going concern assumes the business continues; it does not require showing cost.

options.content: Realisation
options.rationale: Realisation concerns when revenue is recognised.

options.content: Disclosure of full information to users (true and fair view)
options.rationale: Correct: users see what was paid and how much has been used.

options.content: Money measurement
options.rationale: All three figures are in money anyway.

parts.explanation: Showing cost and accumulated depreciation gives users a fuller, fairer picture.

explanation: This item practises calculating and presenting depreciation from a trial balance.

stem: Equipment cost US\$16,000 and its provision for depreciation is US\$6,400. What is its net book value?

options.rationale: Cost and provision were added instead of subtracted.
This is the provision, not the net book value.
This is the cost.

explanation: Net book value = cost − accumulated depreciation = 16,000 − 6,400 = 9,600.

stem: Give the name of the account that is credited each year with the depreciation charge.
explanation: The provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account is credited.
